title: Surfing App
subtitle: A mobile telemetry and progression system designed to help surfers track wave mechanics before, during, and after a session.

caseSections.label: Context & Friction
caseSections.content:
Surfing relies heavily on environmental intuition, yet existing digital tools isolate telemetry data to pre-session planning.

Surfers check their phones on the beach, but once they enter the water, the feedback loop breaks.

This project explores an interruption-tolerant mobile ecosystem designed for the hostile environment of the ocean. The challenge was designing an interface that surfers could interact with under extreme physical constraints (glare, water, motion) without breaking their state of flow, while simultaneously solving the high barrier to entry for tourists navigating expensive local coaching networks.

caseSections.label: Systems Analysis
caseSections.content:
Behavioral Gap Analysis: The Pre-Entry Wall

Using Synthetic Users for rapid AI-simulated interviews, followed by contextual field studies, I mapped the complete user journey to identify where the data loop failed.

Session PhaseUser BehaviorSystem FrictionThe Design Opportunity
Pre-EntryAggressively checks wind, tide, and swell data.High cognitive load; attempting to memorize patterns.Session Setup Swipe: A single-action, high-contrast lock screen that initiates passive background telemetry.
Active SessionRelies entirely on physical intuition; device is locked or left behind.Wet screens and extreme glare render standard UI completely unusable.Glanceable Architecture: Absolute black-and-white contrast prioritizing a single metric per screen; edge-to-edge swipe targets.
Post-SessionAttempts to recall specific waves or tricks to track progression.Memory degradation; tourists lack local knowledge to benchmark against.Gamified Progression Journaling: Correlating time-stamped tricks with localized wave data to map unknown patterns.

caseSections.label: Testing & Constraints
caseSections.content:
Testing Pivots & The Reality of the Environment

Because of the tight 8-week timeline, I moved rapidly from "Crazy Eights" ideation directly into mid-fidelity greyscale testing in Figma to stress-test the interaction models.

Concept TestedUser / Environmental FeedbackStrategic Pivot
Voice AI (Agentic Feedback)Users reported their own voices sound muffled or trapped in their heads while surfing. Audio models failed against wave noise.Abandoned Voice UI: Despite the 2024 trend of AI agents, I stripped out voice entirely in favor of high-contrast visual continuity.
High-Contrast Motion UISenior stakeholders noted the specific color contrasts combined with moving water induced motion sickness (hallucinations).WCAG Motion Calibration: Recalibrated the color system and contrast ratios to meet strict accessibility standards for aquatic motion.
Hardware AgnosticismA user tested the prototype on a folding Samsung flip phone, completely breaking the standard tap targets.Responsive Constraints: Acknowledged the severe impact of unique form factors on touch targets, logging it as a critical v2 requirement while locking v1 to a standard viewport.

caseSections.label: Solution Architecture
caseSections.content:
The Architecture of Session-Based Continuity

Good UX is not just about the screen you are on; it is about how the system remembers where you were. I engineered the app around Session-Based Continuity. Information does not carry over unnecessarily, but the active state never resets until manually stopped.

This architecture solved the core problem of aquatic lockouts. It allowed for the integration of a localized equipment marketplace and video coaching module—bypassing expensive local tourist traps—by keeping the user anchored in a single, continuous retention loop from the beach, to the water, and back to the journal.

caseSections.label: Outcome & Reflection
caseSections.content: The final system turns a fragmented pre-session tool into one interruption-tolerant journey: setup on the beach, passive continuity in the water, and meaningful progression afterward.

solution.content:
How can wave tracking survive the friction of an active surf session?

Surfing depends heavily on environmental intuition. Most digital surf tools help users prepare before entering the water, but the moment the session begins, the feedback loop breaks.

This project explores a mobile ecosystem designed around that gap. It connects predictive ocean data, active session tracking, personal progression, and local surf support into one continuous experience.

The challenge was not simply to design another sports-tracking app. It was to design an interface that could survive glare, water, motion, interrupted attention, and the physical rhythm of surfing without breaking the user’s state of flow.

Hero visual slot: phone mockup, wave map, telemetry overlay, or animated session screen

Behavioral Research

Understanding how surfers interact with digital tools before, during, and after a session.

Environmental Prototyping

Testing how glare, water, motion, and touch inaccuracy affect interface decisions.

Session-Based Continuity

Designing a system that preserves context across interrupted, fragmented interactions.

An interruption-tolerant tracking system built for the water.

The Surfing App is a conceptual mobile platform that tracks wave mechanics and physical performance through a simplified, high-contrast interface.

The product is structured around session-based continuity. Instead of treating every screen as a separate interaction, the app preserves the active session state until the user manually ends it.

This allows the surfer to interact in short bursts without losing context. The system also extends beyond active tracking through progression journaling, embedded tutorials, and localized equipment rentals.

Session-Based Continuity

The app preserves active session data without requiring manual saves. This matters because surfers interact with devices in short, interrupted moments and cannot afford to restart tracking logic mid-session.

Glanceable Telemetry

The interface prioritizes one key metric at a time. It avoids dense dashboards because bright sunlight, movement, and water droplets make complex UI layouts harder to read.

Progression Journaling and Embedded Classes

Users can log named tricks, review personal bests, and access video tutorials. The app becomes a learning system, not just a tracking surface.

Localized Equipment Marketplace

The app connects users to local surf shops for rentals and gear access. This reduces friction for tourists who often face hidden charges or fragmented local information.

Solution visual slot: final app screens, onboarding flow, active tracking UI, progression journal, rental module

flows.content:
The experience is built around two high-friction moments: entering the water and returning from it.

The core flows were designed to reduce interaction during the session and move deeper reflection to the moment after the surfer returns to land.

Flow 1: Session Setup

Trigger: The user initiates a new surf session on the beach.

Action: The user defines location and targets with a simple setup interaction.

System response: The app locks the screen for water use and begins background telemetry.

Value: It removes pre-entry friction and prevents accidental touches in the water.

Flow 2: Skill Progression Logging

Trigger: The user completes a session and returns to land.

Action: The user reviews telemetry and logs named tricks.

System response: The app connects trick timestamps with localized wave-pattern data.

Value: It builds a personal progression journal and contributes to long-term wave behavior mapping.

Flow 3: Equipment and Learning Support

Trigger: A tourist or beginner needs gear, lessons, or skill guidance.

Action: The user browses trusted rental options or embedded learning content.

System response: The app surfaces localized support without relying on informal networks.

Value: It reduces the cost and trust barrier around surf coaching and rentals.

Flow visual slot: journey map, app flow diagram, session loop animation, or wireflow

research.content:
Users checked their phones before entering the water, then abandoned the interface completely.

To understand the friction points of aquatic tech use, the research combined rapid early validation with deeper behavioral observation.

Synthetic Users were used to generate early interview patterns and pressure-test assumptions. These were followed by contextual inquiry and diary-style observation to understand how surfers actually behave before, during, and after sessions.

Method: Contextual Inquiry

Used to understand the physical and environmental conditions around surf preparation, device use, and session entry.

Method: Diary Studies

Used to observe patterns across sessions rather than relying only on one-time recall.

Method: Synthetic User AI Testing

Used for rapid early validation and to identify possible friction points before moving into grounded research.

Method: Quantitative Behavioral Parsing

Used to make sense of repeated behavioral patterns and translate them into product decisions.

Research visual slot: observation notes, journey mapping, research synthesis clusters, or insight cards

The Pre-Entry Wall

Users leave devices behind because current interfaces are not usable when wet. The design implication was clear: the app needed an aquatic lock state and passive tracking capabilities.

The Coaching Cost Barrier

Tourists and beginners often navigate steep costs, hidden charges, and unreliable local networks. This shaped the decision to include tutorials and trusted rental access.

The Voice UI Trap

Voice interaction seemed relevant at first, but the surfing environment made it unreliable. The final interface avoids voice input and depends on visual clarity instead.

formFactors.content:
The project shifted from feature density to environmental restraint.

Early exploration focused on how much information the app should expose during a session. The strongest direction was not the one with the most features, but the one that asked the least from the user while they were physically engaged with the water.

Audio-First Feedback

What it was: A waterproof earbud-based flow that delivered wave stats through an AI voice layer.

Why it seemed promising: It bypassed the screen visibility problem completely.

Why it changed: Ocean acoustics made voice input and feedback unreliable. Repeating commands would break concentration and increase frustration.

High-Density Dashboard

What it was: A data-heavy screen showing wind, swell, tide, and performance metrics together.

Why it seemed promising: It gave the user more control over environmental variables.

Why it changed: It caused too much cognitive load during the session and became harder to read in glare and motion.

Simplified Visual Telemetry

Where the direction landed: The final direction prioritizes one metric at a time through a high-contrast interface, while the system architecture remembers the larger session context in the background.

Exploration visual slot: rejected voice UI concept, dense dashboard concept, simplified telemetry comparison

prototyping.content:
Testing revealed that visibility was not only about contrast. It was about motion, context, and device behavior.

Due to the eight-week timeline, the project moved quickly from ideation into mid-fidelity prototyping. Crazy Eights was used for rapid concept generation, Relume supported early information architecture, and Figma was used to build testable greyscale prototypes.

The goal was not to perfect visual design early. It was to expose the interaction model to physical and behavioral stress as quickly as possible.

Prototype visual slot: Figma mid-fidelity screens, greyscale flow, or before-after interface iterations

Testing Insight 1: High contrast can still create discomfort

Senior stakeholders noted that the initial high-contrast palette could induce motion discomfort or visual vibration in moving water. The color system was recalibrated to reduce harshness while retaining legibility.

Testing Insight 2: Hardware variation changes the interaction model

One user attempted to interact with the prototype on a folded Samsung flip phone. This revealed that aquatic hardware constraints go beyond waterproofing. Form factor, viewport, and touch target behavior need to be treated as future design requirements.

Testing Insight 3: Scope had to protect the core interaction

The first version remained locked to a standard viewport so the session logic could be resolved clearly before expanding into responsive edge cases.

decisions.content:
The final design was shaped by environmental realities, not interface trends.

Decision 1: Preserve the session until the user ends it

Problem: Users frequently lose context when an app auto-locks, reloads, or resets during physical activity.

Options considered: Standard app state management versus persistent background session logic.

Final decision: The active state remains continuous until manually stopped.

Rationale: This mirrors the mental model of surfing as one continuous physical session.

Tradeoff: It requires more complex backend state logic.

Decision 2: Remove AI voice interaction

Problem: Users cannot easily look at screens while paddling or moving through water.

Options considered: Voice agents versus high-contrast visual feedback.

Final decision: Voice interaction was removed entirely.

Rationale: Muffled acoustics and ocean noise made voice models too unreliable for this context.

Tradeoff: The user still needs occasional visual attention, but the system avoids misinterpreted commands.

Decision 3: Include the market ecosystem lightly

Problem: Tourists face hidden charges when seeking coaching or renting surf equipment.

Options considered: A pure telemetry app versus an integrated support ecosystem.

Final decision: The app includes a lightweight rental and embedded video class module.

Rationale: It responds to a real pain point while giving the product a stronger retention loop.

Tradeoff: It increases the information architecture scope.

Design decision visual slot: system logic diagram, voice UI rejection diagram, or feature tradeoff matrix

hardware.content:
Designing for an interface that is wet, glaring, and moving.

The interface had to respond to a hostile environment. The screen was not treated as a stable surface. It was treated as something affected by water, glare, inaccurate touch, interruptions, and body movement.

Eight-Week Time Constraint

The timeline limited the ability to design a fully responsive ecosystem from day one. The first version stayed locked to a single viewport so the core session logic could be resolved well.

High Glare

Sunlight makes subtle UI elements disappear. The interface removed soft grayscale dependence and moved toward stronger contrast and clearer hierarchy.

Touch Inaccuracy

Wet fingers and screens increase mis-taps. Standard tap targets were replaced by larger, simpler interaction zones where possible.

Constraint visual slot: glare test, wet-screen touch diagram, hardware stress states, or responsive notes

reflection.content:
Moving from screen-led to context-led design.

Scoping against trends

This project reinforced the importance of ignoring industry trends when the context demands it. Voice AI was a strong trend during the project, but the ocean made it unreliable. The best technology was not the most current one. It was the one that worked in the user’s environment.

Designing for hostile environments

The surfing context forced the interface to become more disciplined. Decorative UI had to be stripped away because every pixel needed to support visibility, orientation, or action.

Systems thinking in state management

The strongest learning was that good UX is not only about the screen in front of the user. It is also about how the system remembers what the user was doing. Session-based continuity became the anchor of the entire product.

This project clarified a larger design belief: digital architecture should adapt to human behavior, instead of forcing people to adapt to the screen.

title: Kaari
subtitle: A service ecosystem and physical hardware product that connects artisans directly to buyers across language barriers.
pageTitle: Kaari Service Design Ecosystem | Areen Pednekar
metaDescription: A comprehensive service design and hardware case study exploring how native audio terminals and integrated logistics can bypass middlemen in the artisanal craft sector.
previewText: Connecting buyers directly to craftsmen by replacing screens with a dust-resistant native-audio terminal.

caseSections.label: Context & Friction
caseSections.content:
The artisanal supply chain is fundamentally broken by a reliance on middlemen.

Buyers—such as design students, boutique owners, and export houses—struggle to communicate directly with karigars (craftsmen) due to severe language barriers and logistical friction. Consequently, brokers step in, taking a massive percentage of the profit simply to act as translators and shippers.

Kaari is a holistic service design intervention that bridges the gap between modern e-commerce and traditional, dusty workshops. The challenge was not just building a digital app, but designing a dual-sided platform paired with a physical hardware device that speaks the artisan's native language—rendering the broker entirely obsolete without forcing the artisan to become a digital expert.

caseSections.label: Systems Analysis
caseSections.content:
Qualitative Systems Analysis: The Middleman Tax

Our initial ethnographic research mapped the existing business model against the proposed Kaari ecosystem to isolate where value was being lost.

Workflow StageTraditional Broker ModelThe Kaari Ecosystem Model
Order IntakeBuyer contacts broker; broker travels to workshop to translate the brief.Buyer submits digital spec sheet; translated instantly via Kaari API.
CommunicationDependent on the broker's availability and translation accuracy.Direct native-audio announcements broadcasted on the workshop floor.
LogisticsBroker manually collects and ships the finished product, charging a premium.Automated API trigger dispatches Porter/Dunzo directly to the workshop.
Margin RetentionArtisan retains ~40–50% of the true project value.Artisan retains 100% of the fabrication value, minus standard SaaS/API fees.

caseSections.label: Testing & Constraints
caseSections.content:
Ethnographic Realities & Environmental Constraints

Research was conducted not via surveys, but through deep field studies on the workshop floor. We observed that existing digital platforms assumed high digital literacy and English proficiency, making them entirely useless in a noisy, high-heat environment.

ObservationImplicationDesign Pivot
The "Paytm Box" Mental ModelArtisans trust and rely on audio-based payment confirmation boxes to verify transactions without stopping physical labor.The Audio Handoff: We abandoned screen-heavy tablets for the artisan, pivoting to a native-audio terminal that reads orders aloud in local dialects.
The Workshop EnvironmentHeavy dust, micro-particles, and high heat destroy standard consumer electronics rapidly.Industrial Design Constraints: Modeled and 3D-printed a sealed, CMF-optimized hardware terminal with minimal crevices and robust thermal management.
Digital Admin AversionTraditional form-filling causes severe drop-off during onboarding; artisans prefer physical labor over admin.API Trust Bridge: Integrated DigiLocker and Aadhaar APIs for instant, paperless verification to build immediate trust.

caseSections.label: Solution Architecture
caseSections.content:
The Hardware-Software Bridge

Testing physical mockups in the workshop proved that screens fail when hands are covered in dust. I modeled and 3D-printed a sleek, sealed hardware terminal that sits in the workspace.

When a buyer places a custom order through the modern Kaari app, the physical terminal lights up and announces the order details in the karigar's native language. The artisan accepts the job via a tactile, dust-proof button. Once fabrication is complete, hitting a second tactile trigger pings the Dunzo/Porter API, dispatching a driver for final-mile logistics.

caseSections.label: Outcome & Reflection
caseSections.content:
Outcome & Strategic Reflection

Kaari culminated in a thoroughly validated service ecosystem featuring a tested digital application and a functional 3D-printed hardware prototype. By stepping off the screen and into the physical reality of the user, this project proved that true innovation happens when you stop forcing users to learn your interface, and instead build an ecosystem that survives their reality.

solution.content:
How do you digitize an artisan's business without forcing them to become digital experts?

The artisanal supply chain is dominated by middlemen. Buyers, such as design students and boutique owners, struggle to communicate directly with karigars (craftsmen) due to severe language barriers and logistical friction. Kaari is a holistic service design intervention bridging the gap between modern e-commerce and traditional, dusty workshops.

The challenge was designing a dual-sided digital platform paired with a physical hardware device that speaks the artisan's native language, completely rendering the broker obsolete.

Ethnographic Research

Spending time in karigar workshops to understand physical and linguistic constraints.

Hardware Prototyping

Designing and 3D-printing a dust-resistant audio terminal for the workshop floor.

Ecosystem Design

Connecting buyer apps, artisan hardware, and third-party logistics into one seamless service.

Language barriers create a dependency on brokers who erode artisan profits.

When buyers from large export houses or design schools need custom work, they cannot easily communicate with the actual craftsmen. The karigars rely heavily on their native language and traditional manual workflows. This forces the introduction of a middleman to translate and manage orders.

This broker ends up taking a massive percentage of the profit. The visible symptom was a lack of direct digital commerce for artisans. The deeper underlying issue was that existing digital platforms assumed high digital literacy and English proficiency, making them entirely useless on a noisy, dusty workshop floor.

Build technology that adapts to the workshop, not the other way around.

Observing karigars successfully use audio-based payment confirmation boxes revealed a massive opportunity. We could use that exact mental model for order management, replacing screens with sound.

Opportunity 1

Translate digital text orders into native audio announcements on the workshop floor.

Opportunity 2

Create a dual-interface ecosystem where buyers use a modern app and artisans use a rugged hardware terminal.

Opportunity 3

Unify the fragmented delivery process by integrating third-party logistics APIs.

A combined hardware and software service that translates orders into spoken native dialects.

Kaari is a complete service ecosystem. It features a consumer-facing app for buyers to place detailed custom orders, an artisan-facing backend for business management, and a physical hardware terminal designed for the workshop. I led the client app flows, the artisan logic, and the CAD modeling for the physical device.

The hardware sits in the workspace and announces incoming orders and updates in the karigar's native language, bypassing the need to read screens, hire translators, or surrender profit margins.

Native Audio Announcements

What it does: Translates digital app orders into spoken local dialects through the hardware device.

Why it matters: It eliminates the language barrier and keeps the craftsman's hands free.

Dust-Resistant Hardware

What it does: A sleek, 3D-printed physical terminal engineered with minimal crevices.

Why it matters: Standard electronics fail rapidly in high-dust, high-heat artisanal workshops.

Integrated Logistics API

What it does: Connects finished orders directly to delivery networks like Dunzo and Porter.

Why it matters: It automates the physical handoff, removing the burden of shipping from the artisan.

Secure Digital Onboarding

What it does: Utilizes DigiLocker and national ID systems to verify artisans quickly.

Why it matters: It replaces heavy administrative paperwork with instant, trusted verification.

Final solution visual slot: high-fidelity app screens highlighting the earthy UI tones and fast digital ID onboarding flow

flows.content:
The Custom Order Request

Trigger: A buyer needs a custom piece fabricated.

Action: The user inputs specifications, reference images, and material requests into the Kaari app.

System response: The system structures the request and routes it to an appropriate artisan's queue.

Value: It standardizes custom requests without requiring a broker to negotiate terms.

The Artisan Hardware Handoff

Trigger: A new order reaches the artisan's digital queue.

Action: The physical terminal lights up and announces the order details out loud in the artisan's native language.

System response: The artisan accepts the job via a tactile button on the device.

Value: It respects the craftsman's existing technological comfort zone and keeps them focused on their physical labor.

Automated Logistics Dispatch

Trigger: The artisan marks the physical product as complete on the terminal.

Action: The system automatically pings a third-party delivery partner.

System response: A driver is dispatched directly to the workshop for pickup and delivery to the buyer.

Value: It removes the final logistical hurdle, making the artisan fully independent.

Flow visual slot: system architecture map showing how the Buyer App, Artisan Hardware, and Dunzo API connect

research.content:
The most valuable insights came from the workshop floor, not a survey.

The research phase relied on deep ethnography. We went directly into the homes and workspaces of karigars, while also conducting qualitative interviews with fashion, product, and interior design students who frequently source artisanal work.

Methods Used

Contextual Inquiry & Field Studies

User Interviews

Usability Testing

The Audio Precedent

What it revealed: Artisans were highly comfortable with audio-based smart devices because they do not require stopping manual labor to read a screen.

Design implication: Order management needed a hardware component that relied on native audio feedback rather than a purely screen-based UI.

The Middleman Tax

What it revealed: Middlemen exist primarily to bridge the language and logistics gap, not to add value to the craft itself.

Design implication: The service needed integrated translation and automated delivery to render the middleman obsolete.

The Environmental Reality

What it revealed: Standard electronics fail or degrade quickly in artisan workshops due to severe dust and heat.

Design implication: The physical terminal required a highly specific CMF (Color, Materials, Finish) strategy to remain sealed and functional.

Research visual slot: ethnography photos showing the dusty workshop environment and the karigars at work

formFactors.content:
Engineering a form factor for heat, dust, and heavy use.

Screen-Heavy Tablet App

What it was: A ruggedized tablet given to artisans to manage their digital storefront.

Why it seemed promising: It allowed for high information density and image viewing.

Why it changed, failed, or evolved: Contextual testing showed artisans could not easily wipe their hands to tap screens constantly. It interrupted their actual craft.

Exposed Speaker Terminal

What it was: A highly perforated smart speaker design.

Why it seemed promising: It maximized audio clarity for the noisy workshop.

Why it changed, failed, or evolved: Mockups left in the workshop collected severe dust in the speaker grille, threatening the internal mechanics.

Where the direction landed

I modeled and 3D-printed a sleek, sealed hardware terminal. It prioritized thermal management and a dust-resistant shell, utilizing minimal tactile buttons and a protected audio output. App exploration focused on earthy tones and highly accessible digital ID integrations to build trust.

prototyping.content:
Validating physical durability and digital accessibility.

The prototyping phase was split between testing the digital application flows with buyers and testing the physical hardware mockups in real artisan environments. I utilized CAD to print structural mockups specifically for environmental stress testing.

Workshop Dust Testing

What happened: We left physical form mockups in active workshops for several days.

What it meant: Micro-particles and dust seeped into standard device seams, confirming that typical consumer electronics would not survive.

What changed in the design: I adjusted the CAD models to create a sleeker, sealed form factor that battled dust accumulation while managing heat dissipation.

Artisan Onboarding Testing

What happened: Early app testing revealed friction during the artisan onboarding process.

What it meant: Traditional form-filling was too tedious for users who preferred physical labor over digital admin.

What changed in the design: We pivoted to integrate automated national ID verification (DigiLocker) to make digital onboarding almost instantaneous.

Prototype visual slot: physical CAD models and 3D prints on a workshop table being tested for dust

decisions.content:
The final ecosystem was shaped by physical realities, not just digital best practices.

Decision 1: Designing Hardware, Not Just Software

Problem: An app alone could not bridge the usability gap on a workshop floor.

Options considered: An artisan-facing mobile app versus a dedicated physical device.

Final decision: Built a bespoke audio hardware terminal.

Rationale: It matched the existing mental model of payment announcers and kept the artisan's hands free.

Tradeoff: It massively increased the complexity of the project by introducing industrial design and manufacturing constraints.

Decision 2: Native Audio Translation

Problem: Buyers and karigars do not speak the same languages.

Options considered: In-app text translation versus localized audio announcements.

Final decision: The hardware device speaks orders out loud in local dialects.

Rationale: It entirely removes the need for literacy or screen time to understand an incoming order.

Tradeoff: Required complex backend integrations for real-time localized text-to-speech.

Decision 3: Outsourcing Logistics

Problem: Artisans do not have time to manage shipping and delivery.

Options considered: Building an internal tracking system versus third-party API integration.

Final decision: Integrated services like Dunzo and Porter directly into the app.

Rationale: It leveraged existing infrastructure to automate the final mile, removing the logistical middleman.

Tradeoff: The service relies heavily on the API reliability of third-party delivery partners.

hardware.content:
Designing ahead of the available technological infrastructure.

API Limitations in 2023

Why it mattered: At the time of development, infrastructure like DigiLocker was still emerging, making seamless digital ID handoffs complex to execute perfectly in a live build.

How the design responded: We had to pitch the integration as a forward-looking architectural concept, designing the user flow for how the APIs would eventually behave at scale rather than limiting the vision to what was strictly available that month.

A comprehensive ecosystem bridging the digital and physical divide.

Kaari culminated in a thoroughly validated service ecosystem featuring a tested digital application and a 3D-printed hardware prototype. The project successfully mapped a realistic route to bypass industry middlemen, empowering artisans to retain their margins while giving buyers direct access to custom craft.

Detail visual slot: close-up render of the final hardware form factor emphasizing the sealed, dust-resistant design

reflection.content:
Service design is about observing invisible systems.

Empathy requires physical presence

You cannot design for an artisan by sitting behind a screen. Being physically present in their workstations, seeing the dust, and hearing the noise fundamentally changed my understanding of what makes a product "usable."

The hardware-software bridge

This project shifted my perspective from pure digital UI to holistic service design. A digital app is useless if the physical environment rejects it. Creating hardware to act as a bridge was the only way to make the software successful.

Kaari cemented my approach to design. True innovation happens when you stop forcing users to learn your interface, and instead build your interface to survive their reality.
